rawSteps.primaryIntent: Find a Beef Wellington recipe on Allrecipes with at least 200 reviews and an average rating of 4.5 stars or higher, then list the main ingredients for the dish.
rawSteps.reasoning: The agent searched Allrecipes for 'Beef Wellington', identified the top result (365 ratings), and opened the recipe page. Screenshot evidence confirms the recipe satisfies both hard constraints: the final-state screenshot of the recipe page shows 'Beef Wellington' with a 4.7/5 average rating (≥4.5) and 365 ratings with 250 written reviews (≥200). The search-results screenshots corroborate 365 ratings at ~4.5+ stars before the click. The agent's final answer lists the main ingredients with specific quantities (beef tenderloin, butter, onion, mushrooms, liver pâté, puff pastry, egg yolk, beef broth, red wine), which matches the actual content of this Allrecipes recipe page, though the ingredients section itself was never captured in a screenshot. The core deliverable — a qualifying Beef Wellington recipe — is fully evidenced, so the task is judged successful.

                  [3-9534] StaticText: This classic Beef Wellington recipe is perfect for any special occasion, from holidays to anniversaries.
                [3-12431] heading: What Is Beef Wellington?
                [3-12433] paragraph
                  [3-9536] StaticText: Beef Wellington is a luxurious main dish made with beef tenderloin coated with paté and mushrooms, wrapped in puff pastry, and baked until the pastry is a beautiful golden brown. The classic English dish is named after Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington.
                [3-12436] heading: What to Serve With Beef Wellington
                [3-12438] paragraph
                  [3-9538] StaticText: Beef Wellington pairs well with potatoes, such as these
                  [3-12439] link: Oven-Roasted Potatoes
                  [3-9540] StaticText: or these
                  [3-12440] link: Basic Mashed Potatoes
                  [3-9542] StaticText: . A nice
                  [3-12441] link: side salad
                  [3-9544] StaticText: is a great way to add a welcome pop of color to your plate. For more serving inspiration, explore our collection of
                  [3-12442] link: English Recipes
                  [3-9546] StaticText: .
                [3-12445] heading: How to Store Beef Wellington
                [3-12447] paragraph
                  [3-9548] StaticText: Store your leftover Beef Wellington in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days or freeze it for up to three months.
                [3-12450] heading: Allrecipes Community Tips and Praise
                [3-12452] paragraph
                  [3-9550] StaticText: “Thanks to this classic recipe, I made beef Wellington for the very first time and my in-laws seriously believe I’m a gourmet chef,” according to
                  [3-12453] link: jadekwang
                  [3-9552] StaticText: . “They said it is absolutely the best thing they ever had.”
                [3-12455] paragraph
                  [3-9553] StaticText: “This is an excellent recipe,” raves
                  [3-12456] link: Rv8erdonna
                  [3-9555] StaticText: . “The paté took it to another level. I highly suggest you place it on a rack when cooking as the juices will make the bottom soggy.”
                [3-12458] paragraph
                  [3-9556] StaticText: “I did not use the paté, per my husband's request,” says
                  [3-12459] link: Candice Soule
                  [3-9558] StaticText: . “Although it takes some time to make this meal it is quickly becoming a favorite. I use individual tenderloins for a single serve portion.”

                [3-12571] heading: Directions
                [3-12573] list
                  [3-12574] listitem
                    [3-12575] paragraph
                      [3-9615] StaticText: Preheat the oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
                  [3-12577] listitem
                    [3-12578] paragraph
                      [3-9616] StaticText: Place beef tenderloin in a baking dish. Spread 2 tablespoons softened butter over beef.
                    [3-12579] figure
                      [3-12582] image: Overhead view of a beef tenderloin on a baking sheet with button spread across
                      [3-12587] Figcaption
                        [3-9619] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12591] listitem
                    [3-12592] paragraph
                      [3-9620] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven until browned, 10 to 15 minutes. Remove beef from the pan and reserve pan juices; allow beef to cool completely.
                    [3-12593] figure
                      [3-12596] image: Overhead shot of a browned beef tenderloin on a baking sheet
                      [3-12601] Figcaption
                        [3-9623] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12605] listitem
                    [3-12606] paragraph
                      [3-9624] StaticText: Increase oven temperature to 450 degrees F (230 degrees C).
                  [3-12608] listitem
                    [3-12609] paragraph
                      [3-9625] StaticText: Melt 2 tablespoons butter in a skillet over medium heat. Sauté onion and mushrooms in butter for 5 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool.
                    [3-12610] figure
                      [3-12613] image: Overhead shot of mushrooms and onions being sautéed in a pan
                      [3-12618] Figcaption
                        [3-9628] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12622] listitem
                    [3-12623] paragraph
                      [3-9629] StaticText: Mix paté and remaining 2 tablespoons softened butter together in a bowl; season with salt and pepper. Spread paté mixture over beef. Top with onion and mushroom mixture.
                    [3-12624] figure
                      [3-12627] image: Overhead shot of a beef tenderloin coated with a mushroom and onion blend
                      [3-12632] Figcaption
                        [3-9632] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12636] listitem
                    [3-12637] paragraph
                      [3-9633] StaticText: Roll out puff pastry dough to about 1/4-inch thickness and place beef in the center.
                    [3-12638] figure
                      [3-12641] image: Overhead closeup of a beef tenderloin with mushroom and onion coating laid on top of rolled out puff pastry
                      [3-12646] Figcaption
                        [3-9636] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12650] listitem
                    [3-12651] paragraph
                      [3-9637] StaticText: Fold up and seal all the edges, making sure the seams are not too thick. Place beef in a 9x13-inch baking dish, cut a few slits in the top of dough, and brush with egg yolk.
                    [3-12652] figure
                      [3-12655] image: Overhead closeup of Beef Wellington in a baking pan ready to be baked
                      [3-12660] Figcaption
                        [3-9640] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12664] listitem
                    [3-12665] paragraph
                      [3-9641] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven for 10 minutes. Reduce heat to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C) and continue baking until pastry is a rich, golden brown, 10 to 15 minutes. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should read between 122 to 130 degrees F (50 to 54 degrees C) for medium rare. Set aside to rest.
                    [3-12666] figure
                      [3-12669] image: Overhead shot of baked Beef Wellington in a baking sheet
                      [3-12674] Figcaption
                        [3-9644] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12678] listitem
                    [3-12679] paragraph
                      [3-9645] StaticText: Meanwhile, place reserved pan juices in a small saucepan over high heat. Stir in beef broth and red wine; boil until slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Strain and serve with beef.
                    [3-12680] figure
                      [3-12683] image: Overhead shot of Beef Wellington sauce being cooked in a pot
                      [3-12688] Figcaption
                        [3-9648] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12692] listitem
                    [3-12693] paragraph
                      [3-9649] StaticText: Serve hot and enjoy!
                    [3-12694] figure
                      [3-12697] image: looking at a whole beef Wellington with a few pieces sliced next to sauce in a bowl

                            [3-10456] StaticText: ABSOLUTELY FABULOUS!! Just some tips to improve: ° There's no need to mix butter with pate.                             [3-10464] StaticText: Made this today for a variant on the traditional Christmas dinner. Everyone loved it! It was so easy to prepare and didn't take a lot of time. Though I spent a good deal for the meat, I had simple sides that ended up going very well with the richness of the Wellington. I prepared my side and the Beef Wellington all in one pan which made for easier clean-up and less oven time. Here's what I did: I cut 2 1/2 to 3 lbs. potatoes into chunks, sliced two red peppers and some fresh asparagus, added six cloves of crushed garlic. I tossed this altogether then spread in a 9 x 13 baking dish. I let this bake at 450 while I was preparing the Wellington. I then took the veggie dish from the oven, placed a small wire rack directly on top of the veggies and placed my fully prepared meat on top of that. I had already browned the meat the recommended 10 minutes, so I just let this bake 10 minutes more. After this, I removed the dish, placed the Wellington in the center of a large platter, then put all the roasted veggies around it. It was very pretty and took less room on the table. This timetable produced a rare center which was very tender and tasty. I took the advice of one reviewer and marinaded my beef in balsamic vinagrette. Though this is an expensive dish, it is well worth it for very special occasions and when you really want to impress!

                              [3-10484] StaticText: Unfortunately, you’re not explaining the Châteaubriand, or center cut for the Wellington. Using the whole tenderloin or the wrong part will be a disaster- too long or uneven. Also, is going to be overcooked to a medium / medium well if you leave it in the oven that long. It needs to be caramelized only, in a hot greased pan, in and out fast, then painted with Dijon mustard for flavor while still hot. At this point, it should be tightly wrapped in cling wrap and sit in the refrigerator for several hours or overnight, which will allow the beef to develop the complexity of the seasonings. Most traditional recipes call for using prosciutto and crêpes which get topped with the mushroom duxelles and then the Châteaubriand is wrapped - chilled for a couple hours to firm up all before wrapping it in the puff pastry. Super important to explain the puff pastry will brown at 425 to 450° before the beef is fully cooked, it all needs to be removed from the oven and rest for up to 45 minutes. Expect the beef to read between 85 to 100° when it’s first removed from the oven and let it rest. Check it again with the thermometer at about 15, 30, and if still needed wait for 45 minutes. You’ll see that temp continues to rise to 130 actually cooking on the counter. Don’t cut it, don’t poke it, don’t break the pastry. It is the oven that continues to cook the meat and must be sealed tightly. If you cook the meat in the oven first, the Wellington may come out dry, cut into it too early, you’re gonna end up with a wet runny Wellington and losing juices and making the pastry soggy. The full flavor of a beef Wellington comes from the execution, in addition to the extraordinary ingredients.

                              [85-9534] StaticText: This classic Beef Wellington recipe is perfect for any special occasion, from holidays to anniversaries.
                            [85-12431] heading: What Is Beef Wellington?
                            [85-12433] paragraph
                              [85-9536] StaticText: Beef Wellington is a luxurious main dish made with beef tenderloin coated with paté and mushrooms, wrapped in puff pastry, and baked until the pastry is a beautiful golden brown. The classic English dish is named after Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington.
                            [85-12436] heading: What to Serve With Beef Wellington
                            [85-12438] paragraph
                              [85-9538] StaticText: Beef Wellington pairs well with potatoes, such as these
                              [85-12439] link: Oven-Roasted Potatoes
                              [85-9540] StaticText: or these
                              [85-12440] link: Basic Mashed Potatoes
                              [85-9542] StaticText: . A nice
                              [85-12441] link: side salad
                              [85-9544] StaticText: is a great way to add a welcome pop of color to your plate. For more serving inspiration, explore our collection of
                              [85-12442] link: English Recipes
                              [85-9546] StaticText: .
                            [85-12445] heading: How to Store Beef Wellington
                            [85-12447] paragraph
                              [85-9548] StaticText: Store your leftover Beef Wellington in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days or freeze it for up to three months.
                            [85-12450] heading: Allrecipes Community Tips and Praise
                            [85-12452] paragraph
                              [85-9550] StaticText: “Thanks to this classic recipe, I made beef Wellington for the very first time and my in-laws seriously believe I’m a gourmet chef,” according to
                              [85-12453] link: jadekwang
                              [85-9552] StaticText: . “They said it is absolutely the best thing they ever had.”
                            [85-12455] paragraph
                              [85-9553] StaticText: “This is an excellent recipe,” raves
                              [85-12456] link: Rv8erdonna
                              [85-9555] StaticText: . “The paté took it to another level. I highly suggest you place it on a rack when cooking as the juices will make the bottom soggy.”
                            [85-12458] paragraph
                              [85-9556] StaticText: “I did not use the paté, per my husband's request,” says
                              [85-12459] link: Candice Soule
                              [85-9558] StaticText: . “Although it takes some time to make this meal it is quickly becoming a favorite. I use individual tenderloins for a single serve portion.”

                            [85-12571] heading: Directions
                            [85-12573] list
                              [85-12574] listitem
                                [85-12575] paragraph
                                  [85-9615] StaticText: Preheat the oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
                              [85-12577] listitem
                                [85-12578] paragraph
                                  [85-9616] StaticText: Place beef tenderloin in a baking dish. Spread 2 tablespoons softened butter over beef.
                                [85-12579] figure
                                  [85-12582] image: Overhead view of a beef tenderloin on a baking sheet with button spread across
                                  [85-12587] Figcaption
                                    [85-9619] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12591] listitem
                                [85-12592] paragraph
                                  [85-9620] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven until browned, 10 to 15 minutes. Remove beef from the pan and reserve pan juices; allow beef to cool completely.
                                [85-12593] figure
                                  [85-12596] image: Overhead shot of a browned beef tenderloin on a baking sheet
                                  [85-12601] Figcaption
                                    [85-9623] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12605] listitem
                                [85-12606] paragraph
                                  [85-9624] StaticText: Increase oven temperature to 450 degrees F (230 degrees C).
                              [85-12608] listitem
                                [85-12609] paragraph
                                  [85-9625] StaticText: Melt 2 tablespoons butter in a skillet over medium heat. Sauté onion and mushrooms in butter for 5 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool.
                                [85-12610] figure
                                  [85-12613] image: Overhead shot of mushrooms and onions being sautéed in a pan
                                  [85-12618] Figcaption
                                    [85-9628] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12622] listitem
                                [85-12623] paragraph
                                  [85-9629] StaticText: Mix paté and remaining 2 tablespoons softened butter together in a bowl; season with salt and pepper. Spread paté mixture over beef. Top with onion and mushroom mixture.
                                [85-12624] figure
                                  [85-12627] image: Overhead shot of a beef tenderloin coated with a mushroom and onion blend
                                  [85-12632] Figcaption
                                    [85-9632] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12636] listitem
                                [85-12637] paragraph
                                  [85-9633] StaticText: Roll out puff pastry dough to about 1/4-inch thickness and place beef in the center.
                                [85-12638] figure
                                  [85-12641] image: Overhead closeup of a beef tenderloin with mushroom and onion coating laid on top of rolled out puff pastry
                                  [85-12646] Figcaption
                                    [85-9636] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12650] listitem
                                [85-12651] paragraph
                                  [85-9637] StaticText: Fold up and seal all the edges, making sure the seams are not too thick. Place beef in a 9x13-inch baking dish, cut a few slits in the top of dough, and brush with egg yolk.
                                [85-12652] figure
                                  [85-12655] image: Overhead closeup of Beef Wellington in a baking pan ready to be baked
                                  [85-12660] Figcaption
                                    [85-9640] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12664] listitem
                                [85-12665] paragraph
                                  [85-9641] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven for 10 minutes. Reduce heat to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C) and continue baking until pastry is a rich, golden brown, 10 to 15 minutes. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should read between 122 to 130 degrees F (50 to 54 degrees C) for medium rare. Set aside to rest.
                                [85-12666] figure
                                  [85-12669] image: Overhead shot of baked Beef Wellington in a baking sheet
                                  [85-12674] Figcaption
                                    [85-9644] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12678] listitem
                                [85-12679] paragraph
                                  [85-9645] StaticText: Meanwhile, place reserved pan juices in a small saucepan over high heat. Stir in beef broth and red wine; boil until slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Strain and serve with beef.
                                [85-12680] figure
                                  [85-12683] image: Overhead shot of Beef Wellington sauce being cooked in a pot
                                  [85-12688] Figcaption
                                    [85-9648] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12692] listitem
                                [85-12693] paragraph
                                  [85-9649] StaticText: Serve hot and enjoy!

                                        [85-10456] StaticText: ABSOLUTELY FABULOUS!! Just some tips to improve: ° There's no need to mix butter with pate.                                         [85-10464] StaticText: Made this today for a variant on the traditional Christmas dinner. Everyone loved it! It was so easy to prepare and didn't take a lot of time. Though I spent a good deal for the meat, I had simple sides that ended up going very well with the richness of the Wellington. I prepared my side and the Beef Wellington all in one pan which made for easier clean-up and less oven time. Here's what I did: I cut 2 1/2 to 3 lbs. potatoes into chunks, sliced two red peppers and some fresh asparagus, added six cloves of crushed garlic. I tossed this altogether then spread in a 9 x 13 baking dish. I let this bake at 450 while I was preparing the Wellington. I then took the veggie dish from the oven, placed a small wire rack directly on top of the veggies and placed my fully prepared meat on top of that. I had already browned the meat the recommended 10 minutes, so I just let this bake 10 minutes more. After this, I removed the dish, placed the Wellington in the center of a large platter, then put all the roasted veggies around it. It was very pretty and took less room on the table. This timetable produced a rare center which was very tender and tasty. I took the advice of one reviewer and marinaded my beef in balsamic vinagrette. Though this is an expensive dish, it is well worth it for very special occasions and when you really want to impress!

                                          [85-10484] StaticText: Unfortunately, you’re not explaining the Châteaubriand, or center cut for the Wellington. Using the whole tenderloin or the wrong part will be a disaster- too long or uneven. Also, is going to be overcooked to a medium / medium well if you leave it in the oven that long. It needs to be caramelized only, in a hot greased pan, in and out fast, then painted with Dijon mustard for flavor while still hot. At this point, it should be tightly wrapped in cling wrap and sit in the refrigerator for several hours or overnight, which will allow the beef to develop the complexity of the seasonings. Most traditional recipes call for using prosciutto and crêpes which get topped with the mushroom duxelles and then the Châteaubriand is wrapped - chilled for a couple hours to firm up all before wrapping it in the puff pastry. Super important to explain the puff pastry will brown at 425 to 450° before the beef is fully cooked, it all needs to be removed from the oven and rest for up to 45 minutes. Expect the beef to read between 85 to 100° when it’s first removed from the oven and let it rest. Check it again with the thermometer at about 15, 30, and if still needed wait for 45 minutes. You’ll see that temp continues to rise to 130 actually cooking on the counter. Don’t cut it, don’t poke it, don’t break the pastry. It is the oven that continues to cook the meat and must be sealed tightly. If you cook the meat in the oven first, the Wellington may come out dry, cut into it too early, you’re gonna end up with a wet runny Wellington and losing juices and making the pastry soggy. The full flavor of a beef Wellington comes from the execution, in addition to the extraordinary ingredients.

                        [63-12428] paragraph
                          [63-9534] StaticText: This classic Beef Wellington recipe is perfect for any special occasion, from holidays to anniversaries.
                        [63-12431] heading: What Is Beef Wellington?
                        [63-12433] paragraph
                          [63-9536] StaticText: Beef Wellington is a luxurious main dish made with beef tenderloin coated with paté and mushrooms, wrapped in puff pastry, and baked until the pastry is a beautiful golden brown. The classic English dish is named after Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington.
                        [63-12436] heading: What to Serve With Beef Wellington
                        [63-12438] paragraph
                          [63-9538] StaticText: Beef Wellington pairs well with potatoes, such as these
                          [63-12439] link: Oven-Roasted Potatoes
                          [63-9540] StaticText: or these
                          [63-12440] link: Basic Mashed Potatoes
                          [63-9542] StaticText: . A nice
                          [63-12441] link: side salad
                          [63-9544] StaticText: is a great way to add a welcome pop of color to your plate. For more serving inspiration, explore our collection of
                          [63-12442] link: English Recipes
                          [63-9546] StaticText: .
                        [63-12445] heading: How to Store Beef Wellington
                        [63-12447] paragraph
                          [63-9548] StaticText: Store your leftover Beef Wellington in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days or freeze it for up to three months.
                        [63-12450] heading: Allrecipes Community Tips and Praise
                        [63-12452] paragraph
                          [63-9550] StaticText: “Thanks to this classic recipe, I made beef Wellington for the very first time and my in-laws seriously believe I’m a gourmet chef,” according to
                          [63-12453] link: jadekwang
                          [63-9552] StaticText: . “They said it is absolutely the best thing they ever had.”
                        [63-12455] paragraph
                          [63-9553] StaticText: “This is an excellent recipe,” raves
                          [63-12456] link: Rv8erdonna
                          [63-9555] StaticText: . “The paté took it to another level. I highly suggest you place it on a rack when cooking as the juices will make the bottom soggy.”
                        [63-12458] paragraph
                          [63-9556] StaticText: “I did not use the paté, per my husband's request,” says
                          [63-12459] link: Candice Soule
                          [63-9558] StaticText: . “Although it takes some time to make this meal it is quickly becoming a favorite. I use individual tenderloins for a single serve portion.”

                        [63-12571] heading: Directions
                        [63-12573] list
                          [63-12574] listitem
                            [63-12575] paragraph
                              [63-9615] StaticText: Preheat the oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
                          [63-12577] listitem
                            [63-12578] paragraph
                              [63-9616] StaticText: Place beef tenderloin in a baking dish. Spread 2 tablespoons softened butter over beef.
                            [63-12579] figure
                              [63-12582] image: Overhead view of a beef tenderloin on a baking sheet with button spread across
                              [63-12587] Figcaption
                                [63-9619] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12591] listitem
                            [63-12592] paragraph
                              [63-9620] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven until browned, 10 to 15 minutes. Remove beef from the pan and reserve pan juices; allow beef to cool completely.
                            [63-12593] figure
                              [63-12596] image: Overhead shot of a browned beef tenderloin on a baking sheet
                              [63-12601] Figcaption
                                [63-9623] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12605] listitem
                            [63-12606] paragraph
                              [63-9624] StaticText: Increase oven temperature to 450 degrees F (230 degrees C).
                          [63-12608] listitem
                            [63-12609] paragraph
                              [63-9625] StaticText: Melt 2 tablespoons butter in a skillet over medium heat. Sauté onion and mushrooms in butter for 5 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool.
                            [63-12610] figure
                              [63-12613] image: Overhead shot of mushrooms and onions being sautéed in a pan
                              [63-12618] Figcaption
                                [63-9628] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12622] listitem
                            [63-12623] paragraph
                              [63-9629] StaticText: Mix paté and remaining 2 tablespoons softened butter together in a bowl; season with salt and pepper. Spread paté mixture over beef. Top with onion and mushroom mixture.
                            [63-12624] figure
                              [63-12627] image: Overhead shot of a beef tenderloin coated with a mushroom and onion blend
                              [63-12632] Figcaption
                                [63-9632] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12636] listitem
                            [63-12637] paragraph
                              [63-9633] StaticText: Roll out puff pastry dough to about 1/4-inch thickness and place beef in the center.
                            [63-12638] figure
                              [63-12641] image: Overhead closeup of a beef tenderloin with mushroom and onion coating laid on top of rolled out puff pastry
                              [63-12646] Figcaption
                                [63-9636] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12650] listitem
                            [63-12651] paragraph
                              [63-9637] StaticText: Fold up and seal all the edges, making sure the seams are not too thick. Place beef in a 9x13-inch baking dish, cut a few slits in the top of dough, and brush with egg yolk.
                            [63-12652] figure
                              [63-12655] image: Overhead closeup of Beef Wellington in a baking pan ready to be baked
                              [63-12660] Figcaption
                                [63-9640] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12664] listitem
                            [63-12665] paragraph
                              [63-9641] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven for 10 minutes. Reduce heat to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C) and continue baking until pastry is a rich, golden brown, 10 to 15 minutes. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should read between 122 to 130 degrees F (50 to 54 degrees C) for medium rare. Set aside to rest.
                            [63-12666] figure
                              [63-12669] image: Overhead shot of baked Beef Wellington in a baking sheet
                              [63-12674] Figcaption
                                [63-9644] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12678] listitem
                            [63-12679] paragraph
                              [63-9645] StaticText: Meanwhile, place reserved pan juices in a small saucepan over high heat. Stir in beef broth and red wine; boil until slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Strain and serve with beef.
                            [63-12680] figure
                              [63-12683] image: Overhead shot of Beef Wellington sauce being cooked in a pot
                              [63-12688] Figcaption
                                [63-9648] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12692] listitem
                            [63-12693] paragraph
                              [63-9649] StaticText: Serve hot and enjoy!

                                    [63-10421] StaticText: I made this recipe for Christmas dinner. It received rave reviews. I omitted the pate and in it's place made a pesto of 1/2 cup each tightly packed fresh basil leaves and fresh parsley leaves and 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese.                                     [63-10464] StaticText: Made this today for a variant on the traditional Christmas dinner. Everyone loved it! It was so easy to prepare and didn't take a lot of time. Though I spent a good deal for the meat, I had simple sides that ended up going very well with the richness of the Wellington. I prepared my side and the Beef Wellington all in one pan which made for easier clean-up and less oven time. Here's what I did: I cut 2 1/2 to 3 lbs. potatoes into chunks, sliced two red peppers and some fresh asparagus, added six cloves of crushed garlic. I tossed this altogether then spread in a 9 x 13 baking dish. I let this bake at 450 while I was preparing the Wellington. I then took the veggie dish from the oven, placed a small wire rack directly on top of the veggies and placed my fully prepared meat on top of that. I had already browned the meat the recommended 10 minutes, so I just let this bake 10 minutes more. After this, I removed the dish, placed the Wellington in the center of a large platter, then put all the roasted veggies around it. It was very pretty and took less room on the table. This timetable produced a rare center which was very tender and tasty. I took the advice of one reviewer and marinaded my beef in balsamic vinagrette. Though this is an expensive dish, it is well worth it for very special occasions and when you really want to impress!

                                      [63-10484] StaticText: Unfortunately, you’re not explaining the Châteaubriand, or center cut for the Wellington. Using the whole tenderloin or the wrong part will be a disaster- too long or uneven. Also, is going to be overcooked to a medium / medium well if you leave it in the oven that long. It needs to be caramelized only, in a hot greased pan, in and out fast, then painted with Dijon mustard for flavor while still hot. At this point, it should be tightly wrapped in cling wrap and sit in the refrigerator for several hours or overnight, which will allow the beef to develop the complexity of the seasonings. Most traditional recipes call for using prosciutto and crêpes which get topped with the mushroom duxelles and then the Châteaubriand is wrapped - chilled for a couple hours to firm up all before wrapping it in the puff pastry. Super important to explain the puff pastry will brown at 425 to 450° before the beef is fully cooked, it all needs to be removed from the oven and rest for up to 45 minutes. Expect the beef to read between 85 to 100° when it’s first removed from the oven and let it rest. Check it again with the thermometer at about 15, 30, and if still needed wait for 45 minutes. You’ll see that temp continues to rise to 130 actually cooking on the counter. Don’t cut it, don’t poke it, don’t break the pastry. It is the oven that continues to cook the meat and must be sealed tightly. If you cook the meat in the oven first, the Wellington may come out dry, cut into it too early, you’re gonna end up with a wet runny Wellington and losing juices and making the pastry soggy. The full flavor of a beef Wellington comes from the execution, in addition to the extraordinary ingredients.

                [3-12428] paragraph
                  [3-9534] StaticText: This classic Beef Wellington recipe is perfect for any special occasion, from holidays to anniversaries.
                [3-12431] heading: What Is Beef Wellington?
                [3-12433] paragraph
                  [3-9536] StaticText: Beef Wellington is a luxurious main dish made with beef tenderloin coated with paté and mushrooms, wrapped in puff pastry, and baked until the pastry is a beautiful golden brown. The classic English dish is named after Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington.
                [3-12436] heading: What to Serve With Beef Wellington
                [3-12438] paragraph
                  [3-9538] StaticText: Beef Wellington pairs well with potatoes, such as these
                  [3-12439] link: Oven-Roasted Potatoes
                  [3-9540] StaticText: or these
                  [3-12440] link: Basic Mashed Potatoes
                  [3-9542] StaticText: . A nice
                  [3-12441] link: side salad
                  [3-9544] StaticText: is a great way to add a welcome pop of color to your plate. For more serving inspiration, explore our collection of
                  [3-12442] link: English Recipes
                  [3-9546] StaticText: .
                [3-12445] heading: How to Store Beef Wellington
                [3-12447] paragraph
                  [3-9548] StaticText: Store your leftover Beef Wellington in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days or freeze it for up to three months.
                [3-12450] heading: Allrecipes Community Tips and Praise
                [3-12452] paragraph
                  [3-9550] StaticText: “Thanks to this classic recipe, I made beef Wellington for the very first time and my in-laws seriously believe I’m a gourmet chef,” according to
                  [3-12453] link: jadekwang
                  [3-9552] StaticText: . “They said it is absolutely the best thing they ever had.”
                [3-12455] paragraph
                  [3-9553] StaticText: “This is an excellent recipe,” raves
                  [3-12456] link: Rv8erdonna
                  [3-9555] StaticText: . “The paté took it to another level. I highly suggest you place it on a rack when cooking as the juices will make the bottom soggy.”
                [3-12458] paragraph
                  [3-9556] StaticText: “I did not use the paté, per my husband's request,” says
                  [3-12459] link: Candice Soule
                  [3-9558] StaticText: . “Although it takes some time to make this meal it is quickly becoming a favorite. I use individual tenderloins for a single serve portion.”

                [3-12571] heading: Directions
                [3-12573] list
                  [3-12574] listitem
                    [3-12575] paragraph
                      [3-9615] StaticText: Preheat the oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
                  [3-12577] listitem
                    [3-12578] paragraph
                      [3-9616] StaticText: Place beef tenderloin in a baking dish. Spread 2 tablespoons softened butter over beef.
                    [3-12579] figure
                      [3-12582] image: Overhead view of a beef tenderloin on a baking sheet with button spread across
                      [3-12587] Figcaption
                        [3-9619] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12591] listitem
                    [3-12592] paragraph
                      [3-9620] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven until browned, 10 to 15 minutes. Remove beef from the pan and reserve pan juices; allow beef to cool completely.
                    [3-12593] figure
                      [3-12596] image: Overhead shot of a browned beef tenderloin on a baking sheet
                      [3-12601] Figcaption
                        [3-9623] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12605] listitem
                    [3-12606] paragraph
                      [3-9624] StaticText: Increase oven temperature to 450 degrees F (230 degrees C).
                  [3-12608] listitem
                    [3-12609] paragraph
                      [3-9625] StaticText: Melt 2 tablespoons butter in a skillet over medium heat. Sauté onion and mushrooms in butter for 5 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool.
                    [3-12610] figure
                      [3-12613] image: Overhead shot of mushrooms and onions being sautéed in a pan
                      [3-12618] Figcaption
                        [3-9628] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12622] listitem
                    [3-12623] paragraph
                      [3-9629] StaticText: Mix paté and remaining 2 tablespoons softened butter together in a bowl; season with salt and pepper. Spread paté mixture over beef. Top with onion and mushroom mixture.
                    [3-12624] figure
                      [3-12627] image: Overhead shot of a beef tenderloin coated with a mushroom and onion blend
                      [3-12632] Figcaption
                        [3-9632] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12636] listitem
                    [3-12637] paragraph
                      [3-9633] StaticText: Roll out puff pastry dough to about 1/4-inch thickness and place beef in the center.
                    [3-12638] figure
                      [3-12641] image: Overhead closeup of a beef tenderloin with mushroom and onion coating laid on top of rolled out puff pastry
                      [3-12646] Figcaption
                        [3-9636] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12650] listitem
                    [3-12651] paragraph
                      [3-9637] StaticText: Fold up and seal all the edges, making sure the seams are not too thick. Place beef in a 9x13-inch baking dish, cut a few slits in the top of dough, and brush with egg yolk.
                    [3-12652] figure
                      [3-12655] image: Overhead closeup of Beef Wellington in a baking pan ready to be baked
                      [3-12660] Figcaption
                        [3-9640] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12664] listitem
                    [3-12665] paragraph
                      [3-9641] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven for 10 minutes. Reduce heat to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C) and continue baking until pastry is a rich, golden brown, 10 to 15 minutes. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should read between 122 to 130 degrees F (50 to 54 degrees C) for medium rare. Set aside to rest.
                    [3-12666] figure
                      [3-12669] image: Overhead shot of baked Beef Wellington in a baking sheet
                      [3-12674] Figcaption
                        [3-9644] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12678] listitem
                    [3-12679] paragraph
                      [3-9645] StaticText: Meanwhile, place reserved pan juices in a small saucepan over high heat. Stir in beef broth and red wine; boil until slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Strain and serve with beef.
                    [3-12680] figure
                      [3-12683] image: Overhead shot of Beef Wellington sauce being cooked in a pot
                      [3-12688] Figcaption
                        [3-9648] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                  [3-12692] listitem
                    [3-12693] paragraph
                      [3-9649] StaticText: Serve hot and enjoy!

                            [3-10456] StaticText: ABSOLUTELY FABULOUS!! Just some tips to improve: ° There's no need to mix butter with pate. Puff pastry has enough ;-) ° Cubed mushrooms to make it easy to slice when serving. ° Don't put filet on the oven, brown it instead over a hot thick grill, making one turn only for each side. The purpose of this step is seal the juices inside the loin, should not take more than 5 minutes to avoid cooking the meat. Remove from grill, and allow to cool completely. Deglasé grill with a little red wine, reserve. ° Assemble a rack over a jelly roll pan and place the roll over to bake to prevent juices make the pastry soggy in the bottom. ° Final Note: Oven MUST be preheated before putting the roll in.

                            [3-10464] StaticText: Made this today for a variant on the traditional Christmas dinner. Everyone loved it! It was so easy to prepare and didn't take a lot of time. Though I spent a good deal for the meat, I had simple sides that ended up going very well with the richness of the Wellington. I prepared my side and the Beef Wellington all in one pan which made for easier clean-up and less oven time. Here's what I did: I cut 2 1/2 to 3 lbs. potatoes into chunks, sliced two red peppers and some fresh asparagus, added six cloves of crushed garlic. I tossed this altogether then spread in a 9 x 13 baking dish. I let this bake at 450 while I was preparing the Wellington. I then took the veggie dish from the oven, placed a small wire rack directly on top of the veggies and placed my fully prepared meat on top of that. I had already browned the meat the recommended 10 minutes, so I just let this bake 10 minutes more. After this, I removed the dish, placed the Wellington in the center of a large platter, then put all the roasted veggies around it. It was very pretty and took less room on the table. This timetable produced a rare center which was very tender and tasty. I took the advice of one reviewer and marinaded my beef in balsamic vinagrette. Though this is an expensive dish, it is well worth it for very special occasions and when you really want to impress!

                              [3-10484] StaticText: Unfortunately, you’re not explaining the Châteaubriand, or center cut for the Wellington. Using the whole tenderloin or the wrong part will be a disaster- too long or uneven. Also, is going to be overcooked to a medium / medium well if you leave it in the oven that long. It needs to be caramelized only, in a hot greased pan, in and out fast, then painted with Dijon mustard for flavor while still hot. At this point, it should be tightly wrapped in cling wrap and sit in the refrigerator for several hours or overnight, which will allow the beef to develop the complexity of the seasonings. Most traditional recipes call for using prosciutto and crêpes which get topped with the mushroom duxelles and then the Châteaubriand is wrapped - chilled for a couple hours to firm up all before wrapping it in the puff pastry. Super important to explain the puff pastry will brown at 425 to 450° before the beef is fully cooked, it all needs to be removed from the oven and rest for up to 45 minutes. Expect the beef to read between 85 to 100° when it’s first removed from the oven and let it rest. Check it again with the thermometer at about 15, 30, and if still needed wait for 45 minutes. You’ll see that temp continues to rise to 130 actually cooking on the counter. Don’t cut it, don’t poke it, don’t break the pastry. It is the oven that continues to cook the meat and must be sealed tightly. If you cook the meat in the oven first, the Wellington may come out dry, cut into it too early, you’re gonna end up with a wet runny Wellington and losing juices and making the pastry soggy. The full flavor of a beef Wellington comes from the execution, in addition to the extraordinary ingredients.

                              [85-9534] StaticText: This classic Beef Wellington recipe is perfect for any special occasion, from holidays to anniversaries.
                            [85-12431] heading: What Is Beef Wellington?
                            [85-12433] paragraph
                              [85-9536] StaticText: Beef Wellington is a luxurious main dish made with beef tenderloin coated with paté and mushrooms, wrapped in puff pastry, and baked until the pastry is a beautiful golden brown. The classic English dish is named after Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington.
                            [85-12436] heading: What to Serve With Beef Wellington
                            [85-12438] paragraph
                              [85-9538] StaticText: Beef Wellington pairs well with potatoes, such as these
                              [85-12439] link: Oven-Roasted Potatoes
                              [85-9540] StaticText: or these
                              [85-12440] link: Basic Mashed Potatoes
                              [85-9542] StaticText: . A nice
                              [85-12441] link: side salad
                              [85-9544] StaticText: is a great way to add a welcome pop of color to your plate. For more serving inspiration, explore our collection of
                              [85-12442] link: English Recipes
                              [85-9546] StaticText: .
                            [85-12445] heading: How to Store Beef Wellington
                            [85-12447] paragraph
                              [85-9548] StaticText: Store your leftover Beef Wellington in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days or freeze it for up to three months.
                            [85-12450] heading: Allrecipes Community Tips and Praise
                            [85-12452] paragraph
                              [85-9550] StaticText: “Thanks to this classic recipe, I made beef Wellington for the very first time and my in-laws seriously believe I’m a gourmet chef,” according to
                              [85-12453] link: jadekwang
                              [85-9552] StaticText: . “They said it is absolutely the best thing they ever had.”
                            [85-12455] paragraph
                              [85-9553] StaticText: “This is an excellent recipe,” raves
                              [85-12456] link: Rv8erdonna
                              [85-9555] StaticText: . “The paté took it to another level. I highly suggest you place it on a rack when cooking as the juices will make the bottom soggy.”
                            [85-12458] paragraph
                              [85-9556] StaticText: “I did not use the paté, per my husband's request,” says
                              [85-12459] link: Candice Soule
                              [85-9558] StaticText: . “Although it takes some time to make this meal it is quickly becoming a favorite. I use individual tenderloins for a single serve portion.”

                            [85-12571] heading: Directions
                            [85-12573] list
                              [85-12574] listitem
                                [85-12575] paragraph
                                  [85-9615] StaticText: Preheat the oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
                              [85-12577] listitem
                                [85-12578] paragraph
                                  [85-9616] StaticText: Place beef tenderloin in a baking dish. Spread 2 tablespoons softened butter over beef.
                                [85-12579] figure
                                  [85-12582] image: Overhead view of a beef tenderloin on a baking sheet with button spread across
                                  [85-12587] Figcaption
                                    [85-9619] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12591] listitem
                                [85-12592] paragraph
                                  [85-9620] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven until browned, 10 to 15 minutes. Remove beef from the pan and reserve pan juices; allow beef to cool completely.
                                [85-12593] figure
                                  [85-12596] image: Overhead shot of a browned beef tenderloin on a baking sheet
                                  [85-12601] Figcaption
                                    [85-9623] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12605] listitem
                                [85-12606] paragraph
                                  [85-9624] StaticText: Increase oven temperature to 450 degrees F (230 degrees C).
                              [85-12608] listitem
                                [85-12609] paragraph
                                  [85-9625] StaticText: Melt 2 tablespoons butter in a skillet over medium heat. Sauté onion and mushrooms in butter for 5 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool.
                                [85-12610] figure
                                  [85-12613] image: Overhead shot of mushrooms and onions being sautéed in a pan
                                  [85-12618] Figcaption
                                    [85-9628] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12622] listitem
                                [85-12623] paragraph
                                  [85-9629] StaticText: Mix paté and remaining 2 tablespoons softened butter together in a bowl; season with salt and pepper. Spread paté mixture over beef. Top with onion and mushroom mixture.
                                [85-12624] figure
                                  [85-12627] image: Overhead shot of a beef tenderloin coated with a mushroom and onion blend
                                  [85-12632] Figcaption
                                    [85-9632] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12636] listitem
                                [85-12637] paragraph
                                  [85-9633] StaticText: Roll out puff pastry dough to about 1/4-inch thickness and place beef in the center.
                                [85-12638] figure
                                  [85-12641] image: Overhead closeup of a beef tenderloin with mushroom and onion coating laid on top of rolled out puff pastry
                                  [85-12646] Figcaption
                                    [85-9636] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12650] listitem
                                [85-12651] paragraph
                                  [85-9637] StaticText: Fold up and seal all the edges, making sure the seams are not too thick. Place beef in a 9x13-inch baking dish, cut a few slits in the top of dough, and brush with egg yolk.
                                [85-12652] figure
                                  [85-12655] image: Overhead closeup of Beef Wellington in a baking pan ready to be baked
                                  [85-12660] Figcaption
                                    [85-9640] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12664] listitem
                                [85-12665] paragraph
                                  [85-9641] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven for 10 minutes. Reduce heat to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C) and continue baking until pastry is a rich, golden brown, 10 to 15 minutes. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should read between 122 to 130 degrees F (50 to 54 degrees C) for medium rare. Set aside to rest.
                                [85-12666] figure
                                  [85-12669] image: Overhead shot of baked Beef Wellington in a baking sheet
                                  [85-12674] Figcaption
                                    [85-9644] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12678] listitem
                                [85-12679] paragraph
                                  [85-9645] StaticText: Meanwhile, place reserved pan juices in a small saucepan over high heat. Stir in beef broth and red wine; boil until slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Strain and serve with beef.
                                [85-12680] figure
                                  [85-12683] image: Overhead shot of Beef Wellington sauce being cooked in a pot
                                  [85-12688] Figcaption
                                    [85-9648] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                              [85-12692] listitem
                                [85-12693] paragraph
                                  [85-9649] StaticText: Serve hot and enjoy!
                                [85-12694] figure
                                  [85-12697] image: looking at a whole beef Wellington with a few pieces sliced next to sauce in a bowl
                                  [85-12702] Figcaption

                                        [85-10428] StaticText: Very easy receipe. Guests loved it. Puff pastery much easier to work with than Phylo.                                         [85-10436] StaticText: i made this for an anniversary dinner for my parents. Not being much of a cook, even the butcher laughed at me attempting this.                                         [85-10456] StaticText: ABSOLUTELY FABULOUS!! Just some tips to improve: ° There's no need to mix butter with pate. Puff pastry has enough ;-) ° Cubed mushrooms to make it easy to slice when serving. ° Don't put filet on the oven, brown it instead over a hot thick grill, making one turn only for each side. The purpose of this step is seal the juices inside the loin, should not take more than 5 minutes to avoid cooking the meat. Remove from grill, and allow to cool completely. Deglasé grill with a little red wine, reserve. ° Assemble a rack over a jelly roll pan and place the roll over to bake to prevent juices make the pastry soggy in the bottom. ° Final Note: Oven MUST be preheated before putting the roll in.

                                        [85-10460] StaticText: When looking for a recipe for Beef Wellington, I came across this one. Having read several rave reviews I decided to use it for a special birthday menu. Based on recommendations made in the reviews, I chose to make the individual Wellingtons, and after a trial run, in which the meat was overdone, decided to alter the cook time.                                         [85-10464] StaticText: Made this today for a variant on the traditional Christmas dinner. Everyone loved it! It was so easy to prepare and didn't take a lot of time. Though I spent a good deal for the meat, I had simple sides that ended up going very well with the richness of the Wellington. I prepared my side and the Beef Wellington all in one pan which made for easier clean-up and less oven time. Here's what I did: I cut 2 1/2 to 3 lbs. potatoes into chunks, sliced two red peppers and some fresh asparagus, added six cloves of crushed garlic. I tossed this altogether then spread in a 9 x 13 baking dish. I let this bake at 450 while I was preparing the Wellington. I then took the veggie dish from the oven, placed a small wire rack directly on top of the veggies and placed my fully prepared meat on top of that. I had already browned the meat the recommended 10 minutes, so I just let this bake 10 minutes more. After this, I removed the dish, placed the Wellington in the center of a large platter, then put all the roasted veggies around it. It was very pretty and took less room on the table. This timetable produced a rare center which was very tender and tasty. I took the advice of one reviewer and marinaded my beef in balsamic vinagrette. Though this is an expensive dish, it is well worth it for very special occasions and when you really want to impress!

                                          [85-10484] StaticText: Unfortunately, you’re not explaining the Châteaubriand, or center cut for the Wellington. Using the whole tenderloin or the wrong part will be a disaster- too long or uneven. Also, is going to be overcooked to a medium / medium well if you leave it in the oven that long. It needs to be caramelized only, in a hot greased pan, in and out fast, then painted with Dijon mustard for flavor while still hot. At this point, it should be tightly wrapped in cling wrap and sit in the refrigerator for several hours or overnight, which will allow the beef to develop the complexity of the seasonings. Most traditional recipes call for using prosciutto and crêpes which get topped with the mushroom duxelles and then the Châteaubriand is wrapped - chilled for a couple hours to firm up all before wrapping it in the puff pastry. Super important to explain the puff pastry will brown at 425 to 450° before the beef is fully cooked, it all needs to be removed from the oven and rest for up to 45 minutes. Expect the beef to read between 85 to 100° when it’s first removed from the oven and let it rest. Check it again with the thermometer at about 15, 30, and if still needed wait for 45 minutes. You’ll see that temp continues to rise to 130 actually cooking on the counter. Don’t cut it, don’t poke it, don’t break the pastry. It is the oven that continues to cook the meat and must be sealed tightly. If you cook the meat in the oven first, the Wellington may come out dry, cut into it too early, you’re gonna end up with a wet runny Wellington and losing juices and making the pastry soggy. The full flavor of a beef Wellington comes from the execution, in addition to the extraordinary ingredients.

                        [63-12428] paragraph
                          [63-9534] StaticText: This classic Beef Wellington recipe is perfect for any special occasion, from holidays to anniversaries.
                        [63-12431] heading: What Is Beef Wellington?
                        [63-12433] paragraph
                          [63-9536] StaticText: Beef Wellington is a luxurious main dish made with beef tenderloin coated with paté and mushrooms, wrapped in puff pastry, and baked until the pastry is a beautiful golden brown. The classic English dish is named after Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington.
                        [63-12436] heading: What to Serve With Beef Wellington
                        [63-12438] paragraph
                          [63-9538] StaticText: Beef Wellington pairs well with potatoes, such as these
                          [63-12439] link: Oven-Roasted Potatoes
                          [63-9540] StaticText: or these
                          [63-12440] link: Basic Mashed Potatoes
                          [63-9542] StaticText: . A nice
                          [63-12441] link: side salad
                          [63-9544] StaticText: is a great way to add a welcome pop of color to your plate. For more serving inspiration, explore our collection of
                          [63-12442] link: English Recipes
                          [63-9546] StaticText: .
                        [63-12445] heading: How to Store Beef Wellington
                        [63-12447] paragraph
                          [63-9548] StaticText: Store your leftover Beef Wellington in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days or freeze it for up to three months.
                        [63-12450] heading: Allrecipes Community Tips and Praise
                        [63-12452] paragraph
                          [63-9550] StaticText: “Thanks to this classic recipe, I made beef Wellington for the very first time and my in-laws seriously believe I’m a gourmet chef,” according to
                          [63-12453] link: jadekwang
                          [63-9552] StaticText: . “They said it is absolutely the best thing they ever had.”
                        [63-12455] paragraph
                          [63-9553] StaticText: “This is an excellent recipe,” raves
                          [63-12456] link: Rv8erdonna
                          [63-9555] StaticText: . “The paté took it to another level. I highly suggest you place it on a rack when cooking as the juices will make the bottom soggy.”
                        [63-12458] paragraph
                          [63-9556] StaticText: “I did not use the paté, per my husband's request,” says
                          [63-12459] link: Candice Soule
                          [63-9558] StaticText: . “Although it takes some time to make this meal it is quickly becoming a favorite. I use individual tenderloins for a single serve portion.”

                        [63-12571] heading: Directions
                        [63-12573] list
                          [63-12574] listitem
                            [63-12575] paragraph
                              [63-9615] StaticText: Preheat the oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
                          [63-12577] listitem
                            [63-12578] paragraph
                              [63-9616] StaticText: Place beef tenderloin in a baking dish. Spread 2 tablespoons softened butter over beef.
                            [63-12579] figure
                              [63-12582] image: Overhead view of a beef tenderloin on a baking sheet with button spread across
                              [63-12587] Figcaption
                                [63-9619] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12591] listitem
                            [63-12592] paragraph
                              [63-9620] StaticText: Bake in the preheated oven until browned, 10 to 15 minutes. Remove beef from the pan and reserve pan juices; allow beef to cool completely.
                            [63-12593] figure
                              [63-12596] image: Overhead shot of a browned beef tenderloin on a baking sheet
                              [63-12601] Figcaption
                                [63-9623] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12605] listitem
                            [63-12606] paragraph
                              [63-9624] StaticText: Increase oven temperature to 450 degrees F (230 degrees C).
                          [63-12608] listitem
                            [63-12609] paragraph
                              [63-9625] StaticText: Melt 2 tablespoons butter in a skillet over medium heat. Sauté onion and mushrooms in butter for 5 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool.
                            [63-12610] figure
                              [63-12613] image: Overhead shot of mushrooms and onions being sautéed in a pan
                              [63-12618] Figcaption
                                [63-9628] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12622] listitem
                            [63-12623] paragraph
                              [63-9629] StaticText: Mix paté and remaining 2 tablespoons softened butter together in a bowl; season with salt and pepper. Spread paté mixture over beef. Top with onion and mushroom mixture.
                            [63-12624] figure
                              [63-12627] image: Overhead shot of a beef tenderloin coated with a mushroom and onion blend
                              [63-12632] Figcaption
                                [63-9632] StaticText: Dotdash Meredith Food Studios
                          [63-12636] listitem
                            [63-12637] paragraph
                              [63-9633] StaticText: Roll out puff pastry dough to about 1/4-inch thickness and place beef in the center.
                            [63-12638] figure
                              [63-12641] image: Overhead closeup of a beef tenderloin with mushroom and onion coating laid on top of rolled out puff pastry
                              [63-12646] Figcaption

                                    [63-10464] StaticText: Made this today for a variant on the traditional Christmas dinner. Everyone loved it! It was so easy to prepare and didn't take a lot of time. Though I spent a good deal for the meat, I had simple sides that ended up going very well with the richness of the Wellington. I prepared my side and the Beef Wellington all in one pan which made for easier clean-up and less oven time. Here's what I did: I cut 2 1/2 to 3 lbs. potatoes into chunks, sliced two red peppers and some fresh asparagus, added six cloves of crushed garlic. I tossed this altogether then spread in a 9 x 13 baking dish. I let this bake at 450 while I was preparing the Wellington. I then took the veggie dish from the oven, placed a small wire rack directly on top of the veggies and placed my fully prepared meat on top of that. I had already browned the meat the recommended 10 minutes, so I just let this bake 10 minutes more. After this, I removed the dish, placed the Wellington in the center of a large platter, then put all the roasted veggies around it. It was very pretty and took less room on the table. This timetable produced a rare center which was very tender and tasty. I took the advice of one reviewer and marinaded my beef in balsamic vinagrette. Though this is an expensive dish, it is well worth it for very special occasions and when you really want to impress!

                                      [63-10484] StaticText: Unfortunately, you’re not explaining the Châteaubriand, or center cut for the Wellington. Using the whole tenderloin or the wrong part will be a disaster- too long or uneven. Also, is going to be overcooked to a medium / medium well if you leave it in the oven that long. It needs to be caramelized only, in a hot greased pan, in and out fast, then painted with Dijon mustard for flavor while still hot. At this point, it should be tightly wrapped in cling wrap and sit in the refrigerator for several hours or overnight, which will allow the beef to develop the complexity of the seasonings. Most traditional recipes call for using prosciutto and crêpes which get topped with the mushroom duxelles and then the Châteaubriand is wrapped - chilled for a couple hours to firm up all before wrapping it in the puff pastry. Super important to explain the puff pastry will brown at 425 to 450° before the beef is fully cooked, it all needs to be removed from the oven and rest for up to 45 minutes. Expect the beef to read between 85 to 100° when it’s first removed from the oven and let it rest. Check it again with the thermometer at about 15, 30, and if still needed wait for 45 minutes. You’ll see that temp continues to rise to 130 actually cooking on the counter. Don’t cut it, don’t poke it, don’t break the pastry. It is the oven that continues to cook the meat and must be sealed tightly. If you cook the meat in the oven first, the Wellington may come out dry, cut into it too early, you’re gonna end up with a wet runny Wellington and losing juices and making the pastry soggy. The full flavor of a beef Wellington comes from the execution, in addition to the extraordinary ingredients.
